statement: For every integer $n \ge 1$ there is a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ with $n < p \le 2n$.

hypotheses.text: The integer $n$ satisfies $n \ge 1$.

proofs.name: Erdős's central binomial proof
proofs.slogan: Compare a lower bound for $\binom{2n}{n}$ with the upper bound that holds when $(n, 2n]$ has no prime, and check small $n$ by a chain of primes.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 1$: the bound comparison covers $n \ge 512$ and a chain of primes covers $1 \le n \le 511$. For $n = 0$ the interval $(0, 0]$ is empty, so the hypothesis is necessary.

roles.why: For $n \ge 1$ the chain of primes starts with $2 \le 2n$, and the two cases cover every such $n$.

steps.slogan: Bound the [central binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) below by $4^n < n\binom{2n}{n}$ for $n \ge 4$.
steps.detail: The binomial theorem gives $\sum_k \binom{2n}{k} = 4^n$, and $\binom{2n}{n}$ is the largest of these $2n + 1$ terms. An induction on $n$ sharpens this count to $4^n < n\binom{2n}{n}$ for $n \ge 4$.

steps.slogan: Show that no prime in $(2n/3, n]$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$.
steps.detail: Let $p$ be such a prime and $n \ge 5$, so $p \le n < 3p/2$ and $p^2 > 2n$. Legendre's formula for the [factorials](c:factorial) $(2n)!$ and $n!^2$ gives the exponent $\lfloor 2n/p \rfloor - 2\lfloor n/p \rfloor = 2 - 2 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound each prime power in $\binom{2n}{n}$ by $2n$, and by $p$ when $p > \sqrt{2n}$.
steps.detail: Legendre's formula gives the exponent $e = \sum_{k \ge 1} (\lfloor 2n/p^k \rfloor - 2\lfloor n/p^k \rfloor)$, with each term $0$ or $1$ and no term once $p^k > 2n$, so $p^e \le 2n$. If $p > \sqrt{2n}$, only $k = 1$ can contribute, so $e \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Assume that no prime lies in $(n, 2n]$ and bound $\binom{2n}{n}$ above.
steps.detail: Then every prime factor of $\binom{2n}{n}$ is at most $2n/3$ by step 2, since primes above $2n$ do not divide it. In the [prime factorization](c:prime-factorization), the primes up to $\sqrt{2n}$ give at most $(2n)^{\sqrt{2n}}$, and the larger ones give at most $\prod_{p \le 2n/3} p \le 4^{2n/3}$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds and get a contradiction for every $n \ge 512$.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 4 give $4^n < n(2n)^{\sqrt{2n}}4^{2n/3}$, that is $4^{n/3} < n(2n)^{\sqrt{2n}}$. A logarithmic estimate shows that this fails for every $n \ge 512$, so some prime lies in $(n, 2n]$.

steps.slogan: Cover each $n \le 511$ by a chain of primes, each less than twice the previous.
steps.detail: In the chain $2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 23, 43, 83, 163, 317, 521$ each prime is less than twice the one before. For $1 \le n \le 511$, the first prime $q$ of the chain with $q > n$ has its predecessor at most $n$ (or $q = 2$), so $q \le 2n$.

steps.slogan: Join the large case and the small case to cover every $n \ge 1$.
steps.detail: Step 5 gives a prime in $(n, 2n]$ for $n \ge 512$, and step 6 gives one for $1 \le n \le 511$. So every $n \ge 1$ has a [prime](c:prime-number) $p$ with $n < p \le 2n$.

concepts.c:prime-number: The theorem asserts a prime in each interval $(n, 2n]$.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The central coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$ is squeezed between two bounds.
concepts.c:factorial: Prime exponents in factorials give the exponents in $\binom{2n}{n}$.
concepts.c:prime-factorization: The upper bound multiplies the prime powers of $\binom{2n}{n}$.

source.note: Nat.bertrand aliases Nat.exists_prime_lt_and_le_two_mul: Nat.four_pow_lt_mul_centralBinom, centralBinom_le_of_no_bertrand_prime (with Nat.factorization_centralBinom_of_two_mul_self_lt_three_mul and primorial_le_four_pow), bertrand_main_inequality for n >= 512, and a chain of primes for small n.

statement: Let $L$ be a nonempty finite [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) and $J$ the [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) of its [join-irreducible elements](c:join-irreducible-element). Then $\phi(a) = \{j \in J : j \le a\}$ is a [lattice isomorphism](c:lattice-hom) from $L$ onto the lattice of [down-sets](c:down-set-2) of $J$, ordered by inclusion.

hypotheses.text: The lattice $L$ is finite and nonempty.
The lattice $L$ is [distributive](c:distributive-lattice): $a \wedge (b \vee c) = (a \wedge b) \vee (a \wedge c)$.

conclusion: The map $\phi$ is a bijection from $L$ onto the down-sets of $J$ that turns joins into unions and meets into intersections.

formal.difference: The declaration gives a lattice homomorphism from L into the power set of its join-irreducibles; that it is a bijection onto the down-sets is OrderIso.lowerSetSupIrred. It also allows the empty lattice.

proofs.name: Join-irreducible decomposition
proofs.slogan: Write each element as the join of the join-irreducibles below it, and use distributivity to show that a join-irreducible below a join lies below one of its terms.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The bottom element maps to the empty down-set, because the bottom is not join-irreducible.

roles.why: Finiteness supports the induction and gives every set of join-irreducibles a join.
Distributivity makes every join-irreducible element join-prime.

steps.slogan: Show that $\phi(a)$ is a [down-set](c:down-set-2) and that $\phi$ preserves order.
steps.detail: If $j \le a$ and $i \le j$ with $i \in J$, then $i \le a$ by transitivity, so $\phi(a)$ is a down-set of $J$. Also $a \le b$ gives $\phi(a) \subseteq \phi(b)$.

steps.slogan: Write every element as the join of the join-irreducibles below it.
steps.detail: Use strong induction on the finite lattice: the bottom is the empty join, and a join-irreducible element is its own join. Any other $a$ equals $b \vee c$ with $b, c < a$, and the decompositions of $b$ and $c$ combine, so $a = \bigvee \phi(a)$.

steps.slogan: Show that a join-irreducible element below a join lies below one of its terms.
steps.detail: Let $j \in J$ with $j \le a \vee b$. [Distributivity](c:distributive-lattice) gives $j = j \wedge (a \vee b) = (j \wedge a) \vee (j \wedge b)$, so $j = j \wedge a$ or $j = j \wedge b$, that is $j \le a$ or $j \le b$.

steps.slogan: Send each down-set $D$ to its join and check that both composites are identities.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives $\bigvee \phi(a) = a$. If $D$ is a down-set and $j \in J$ satisfies $j \le \bigvee D$, then step 3, applied repeatedly to this finite join, gives $j \le d$ for some $d \in D$, so $j \in D$ and $\phi(\bigvee D) = D$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\phi$ turns joins into unions and meets into intersections.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives $\phi(a \vee b) \subseteq \phi(a) \cup \phi(b)$ and step 1 gives the reverse inclusion; $j \le a \wedge b$ holds exactly when $j \le a$ and $j \le b$. So $\phi$ is a bijective [lattice homomorphism](c:lattice-hom) by step 4, hence a lattice isomorphism.

concepts.c:distributive-lattice: Distributivity makes join-irreducibles behave like primes under joins.
concepts.c:partial-order: The join-irreducibles carry the induced partial order of the lattice.
concepts.c:join-irreducible-element: Join-irreducibles are the building blocks of every element.
concepts.c:lattice-hom: The map must preserve joins and meets to be a lattice isomorphism.
concepts.c:down-set-2: Down-sets of join-irreducibles are the images of the lattice elements.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finiteness gives induction and finite joins of join-irreducibles.

source.note: mathlib builds OrderIso.lowerSetSupIrred from exists_supIrred_decomposition and SupIrred.supPrime (join-irreducible means join-prime in a distributive lattice), then derives OrderEmbedding.birkhoffSet_sup and birkhoffSet_inf.

statement: Let $X$ be a real [separable](c:separable-space) [reflexive Banach space](c:reflexive-banach-space) and $T\colon X \to X^*$ a bounded, continuous, [coercive](c:coercive-operator) and [monotone operator](c:monotone-operator). Then $T$ is surjective: for every $g \in X^*$ some $u \in X$ satisfies $T(u) = g$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a real [separable](c:separable-space) [reflexive Banach space](c:reflexive-banach-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$.
The operator $T$ maps bounded sets to bounded sets.
The operator $T$ is continuous from $X$ to $X^*$.
The operator is [coercive](c:coercive-operator): $\langle T(u), u\rangle / \|u\| \to \infty$ as $\|u\| \to \infty$.
The operator is [monotone](c:monotone-operator): $\langle T(u) - T(v), u - v\rangle \ge 0$ for all $u, v \in X$.

conclusion: For every $g \in X^*$ there is $u \in X$ with $T(u) = g$.

proofs.name: Galerkin approximation and Minty's trick
proofs.slogan: Solve the equation on finite-dimensional subspaces by Brouwer's theorem, extract weak limits by reflexivity, and identify the limit by monotonicity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for a fixed $g \in X^*$. Continuity is used only along lines, so the proof also covers hemicontinuous $T$.

roles.why: Separability gives the Galerkin subspaces, and reflexivity gives weakly convergent subsequences.
Boundedness keeps the images $T(u_n)$ in a bounded set, so they have a weak limit.
Continuity makes the finite-dimensional maps continuous and gives $T(u - tw) \to T(u)$.
Coercivity gives one radius $R$, for all $n$, on which the projected map points outward.
Monotonicity gives the limit inequality of Minty's trick.

steps.slogan: Choose finite-dimensional subspaces $X_1 \subseteq X_2 \subseteq \dots$ with dense union.
steps.detail: [Separability](c:separable-space) gives a dense sequence $w_1, w_2, \dots$, and $X_n = \operatorname{span}\{w_1, \dots, w_n\}$ works. Every $v \in X$ is then a limit of elements $v_n \in X_n$.

steps.slogan: Solve the projected equation $\langle T(u_n) - g, v\rangle = 0$ for all $v \in X_n$ by Brouwer's theorem.
steps.detail: Coercivity gives $R$ with $\langle T(u) - g, u\rangle > 0$ whenever $\|u\| = R$. The continuous map $u \mapsto (T(u) - g)|_{X_n}$ from $X_n$ to its dual points outward on the sphere of radius $R$, so the acute-angle corollary of Brouwer's theorem gives a zero $u_n$ with $\|u_n\| \le R$.

steps.slogan: Bound the approximate solutions and their images uniformly in $n$.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives $\|u_n\| \le R$ for every $n$. Because $T$ maps bounded sets to bounded sets, $\|T(u_n)\| \le K$ for one constant $K$.

steps.slogan: Extract a subsequence with $u_n \to u$ and $T(u_n) \to g$ in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology).
steps.detail: [Reflexivity](c:reflexive-banach-space) makes bounded sets of $X$ and of $X^*$ weakly sequentially compact, so a subsequence has $u_n \rightharpoonup u$ and $T(u_n) \rightharpoonup \chi$. For $v \in X_m$ and $n \ge m$, $\langle T(u_n), v\rangle = \langle g, v\rangle$, so $\chi = g$ by density, and $\langle T(u_n), u_n\rangle = \langle g, u_n\rangle \to \langle g, u\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Pass monotonicity to the limit to get $\langle T(v) - g, v - u\rangle \ge 0$ for every $v$.
steps.detail: [Monotonicity](c:monotone-operator) gives $\langle T(v) - T(u_n), v - u_n\rangle \ge 0$ for every $v \in X$. Expand it and let $n \to \infty$: the term $\langle T(u_n), u_n\rangle$ tends to $\langle g, u\rangle$ by step 4, and the other terms converge weakly.

steps.slogan: Insert $v = u - tw$, divide by $t > 0$, and let $t$ tend to zero.
steps.detail: Step 5 gives $\langle T(u - tw) - g, w\rangle \ge 0$ for all $w \in X$ and $t > 0$. Continuity of $T$ gives $\langle T(u) - g, w\rangle \ge 0$, and replacing $w$ by $-w$ yields $T(u) = g$ in the [dual space](c:dual-space).

concepts.c:separable-space: Separability gives the increasing finite-dimensional Galerkin subspaces.
concepts.c:reflexive-banach-space: Reflexivity turns bounded sequences into weakly convergent subsequences.
concepts.c:dual-space: The operator takes values in the dual, where the equation lives.
concepts.c:coercive-operator: Coercivity gives the a priori bound $\|u_n\| \le R$.
concepts.c:monotone-operator: Monotonicity lets weak limits pass through the nonlinear operator.
concepts.c:weak-topology: Only weak limits exist, so the proof works in the weak topology.

source.note: The Galerkin and Minty-trick proof of Browder and Minty, as in E. Zeidler, Nonlinear Functional Analysis and its Applications II/B (Springer, 1990), chapter 26.

statement: A needle of length $l$ falls on a plane ruled by parallel lines at distance $d \ge l$. Its centre's distance to the nearest line is [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) on $[0, d/2]$, its acute angle with the lines is uniform on $[0, \pi/2]$, and the two are [independent](c:independent-random-variables). Then it crosses a line with [probability](c:probability-measure) $2l/(\pi d)$.

hypotheses.text: The needle is not longer than the spacing: $0 < l \le d$.
The distance $x$ is [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) on $[0, d/2]$ and the angle $\theta$ is uniform on $[0, \pi/2]$.
The variables $x$ and $\theta$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables).

conclusion: The probability that the needle meets a line is $2l/(\pi d)$.

proofs.name: Integral over the angle
proofs.slogan: Write the crossing event as $x \le (l/2)\sin\theta$ and integrate the joint density over that region.
proofs.scope: The case $l \le d$. For $l > d$ the curve $x = (l/2)\sin\theta$ leaves the rectangle and the formula changes.

roles.why: It keeps the region under the curve inside the rectangle and allows only one crossed line.
Uniform laws have constant densities $2/d$ and $2/\pi$.
Independence makes the joint density the product of the two densities.

steps.slogan: Express the crossing event as the inequality $x \le (l/2)\sin\theta$.
steps.detail: Each half of the needle reaches a distance $(l/2)\sin\theta$ from its centre, measured across the lines. So the needle meets the nearest line exactly when $x \le (l/2)\sin\theta$; because $l \le d$, it meets no other line except on a null event.

steps.slogan: Write the joint density as $4/(\pi d)$ on the rectangle $[0, d/2] \times [0, \pi/2]$.
steps.detail: Each [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) variable has a constant density, $2/d$ for $x$ and $2/\pi$ for $\theta$. [Independence](c:independent-random-variables) makes the joint density their product $4/(\pi d)$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the joint density over the region below the curve $x = (l/2)\sin\theta$.
steps.detail: The region lies in the rectangle because $(l/2)\sin\theta \le d/2$. Fubini's theorem and the [integral](c:integral) $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin\theta\,d\theta = 1$ give the probability $\frac{4}{\pi d}\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{l}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta = \frac{2l}{\pi d}$.

concepts.c:uniform-distribution: Uniform laws give the constant densities that are integrated.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence makes the joint density a product.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The answer is the probability measure of the crossing event.
concepts.c:integral: The probability is the integral of the density over a region.

source.note: The classical integral computation going back to Buffon (1777), as in most probability texts.

proofs.name: Barbier's noodle argument
proofs.slogan: Show that the expected number of crossings is proportional to length, fix the constant with a circle, and note that a short needle crosses at most once.
proofs.scope: The case $l \le d$, where the crossing count is $0$ or $1$ almost surely. Rigid curves are placed with the same uniform position and angle as the needle.

roles.why: A needle of length at most $d$ meets at most one line, so the probability equals the expected count.
Uniform position and angle make the law of each piece depend only on its length.
Independence lets every piece of a rigid curve carry the same uniform placement.

steps.slogan: Reduce the crossing probability to the expected number $E[N]$ of crossings.
steps.detail: Because $l \le d$, the needle meets at most one line except on a null event, so $N$ takes only the values $0$ and $1$. Hence the crossing probability equals the [expected value](c:expected-value) $E[N]$.

steps.slogan: Show that $E[N] = c\,l$ for needles and rigid polygonal curves by additivity.
steps.detail: Cut a segment into pieces: each piece is placed by the same uniform law, and linearity of expectation gives $E[N(l_1 + l_2)] = E[N(l_1)] + E[N(l_2)]$. A monotone additive function of length is linear, so $E[N] = c\,l$, and summing over sides gives $E[N] = c\,L$ for a rigid polygon of length $L$.

steps.slogan: Compute the constant with a circle of diameter $d$, which always meets the lines twice.
steps.detail: A circle of diameter $d$ meets the lines in exactly two points almost surely. Inscribed and circumscribed polygons satisfy $N_{\mathrm{in}} \le 2 \le N_{\mathrm{out}}$, so $c L_{\mathrm{in}} \le 2 \le c L_{\mathrm{out}}$, and both lengths tend to $\pi d$; hence $c = 2/(\pi d)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the constant with the reduction to get the probability $2l/(\pi d)$.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give the probability $E[N] = c\,l$ for the needle. With $c = 2/(\pi d)$ from step 3, the needle crosses a line with [probability](c:probability-measure) $2l/(\pi d)$.

concepts.c:uniform-distribution: Uniform placement makes the expected count depend only on length.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independent position and angle give every piece the same placement law.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The crossing probability equals the expected number of crossings here.
concepts.c:expected-value: Expected crossing counts add over the pieces of a curve.

source.note: Barbier's 1860 argument (Buffon's noodle), as in M. Aigner and G. M. Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK, chapter on Buffon's needle problem.

statement: Let $\mu$ be [Wiener measure](c:wiener-measure) on $C_0[0, 1]$ and let $h$ lie in the [Cameron-Martin space](c:cameron-martin-space) $H$, the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) of absolutely continuous $h$ with $h(0) = 0$ and $h' \in L^2$. Then $\mu_h(A) = \mu(A - h)$ is [equivalent](c:equivalent-measure) to $\mu$, with [Radon-Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) $\frac{d\mu_h}{d\mu}(\omega) = \exp\big(\int_0^1 h'\,d\omega - \frac12\int_0^1 h'(t)^2\,dt\big)$.

hypotheses.text: The measure $\mu$ is [Wiener measure](c:wiener-measure), the law of Brownian motion on $C_0[0, 1]$.
The shift $h$ is absolutely continuous with $h(0) = 0$ and $\int_0^1 h'(t)^2\,dt < \infty$.

conclusion: The measures $\mu_h$ and $\mu$ are equivalent, and $d\mu_h/d\mu = \exp(\int_0^1 h'\,d\omega - \frac12\|h'\|_{L^2}^2)$.

proofs.name: Finite-dimensional distributions
proofs.slogan: Show that weighting $\mu$ by the proposed density gives a measure whose finite-dimensional distributions are those of $\omega + h$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem on $[0, 1]$. It does not prove the converse fact that $\mu_h$ and $\mu$ are mutually singular when $h \notin H$.

roles.why: Under Wiener measure the coordinates have independent centred Gaussian increments, which builds the Wiener integral.
The condition $h' \in L^2$ makes $\int h'\,d\omega$ exist, and $\int_0^t h' = h(t)$ gives the covariances.

steps.slogan: Define the Wiener integral $I(f) = \int_0^1 f\,d\omega$ for $f \in L^2$ as a Gaussian variable.
steps.detail: For a step function $f = \sum_i c_i 1_{(t_i, t_{i+1}]}$, set $I(f) = \sum_i c_i(\omega(t_{i+1}) - \omega(t_i))$; then $E[I(f)^2] = \|f\|_{L^2}^2$. This isometry extends $I$ to $L^2$, and finite families $(I(f_k))$ are centred jointly Gaussian with covariances $\int f_k f_l\,dt$.

steps.slogan: Check that $Z = \exp(I(h') - \frac12\|h'\|^2)$ is positive and has mean one.
steps.detail: Because $I(h')$ is normal with mean $0$ and variance $\|h'\|^2$, $E[e^{I(h')}] = e^{\|h'\|^2/2}$. So $E[Z] = 1$, $Z > 0$, and $d\nu = Z\,d\mu$ is a probability measure.

steps.slogan: Compute the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of $(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_k))$ under $\nu$.
steps.detail: Put $Y = \sum_j \lambda_j\omega(t_j) = I(f)$ with $f = \sum_j \lambda_j 1_{[0, t_j]}$. For the centred Gaussian pair, $E[e^{I(h') + iY}] = \exp(\frac12\|h'\|^2 - \frac12 E[Y^2] + i\int f h')$ with $\int f h' = \sum_j \lambda_j h(t_j)$, so $E_\nu[e^{iY}] = \exp(i\sum_j \lambda_j h(t_j) - \frac12 E[Y^2])$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\nu$ with $\mu_h$ through their finite-dimensional distributions.
steps.detail: Step 3 is the characteristic function of $(\omega(t_j) + h(t_j))_j$ under $\mu$, so $\nu$ and $\mu_h$ agree on cylinder sets. Cylinder sets form a $\pi$-system that generates the Borel sets of $C_0[0, 1]$, so Dynkin's theorem gives $\nu = \mu_h$; both are [Gaussian measures](c:gaussian-measure) with the same covariance.

steps.slogan: Conclude equivalence from the positive density $Z$.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives $\mu_h(A) = \int_A Z\,d\mu$, so $\mu_h \ll \mu$ with derivative $Z$. Because $Z > 0$ by step 2, also $\mu(A) = \int_A Z^{-1}\,d\mu_h$, so the measures are [equivalent](c:equivalent-measure).

concepts.c:wiener-measure: The theorem shifts Wiener measure and compares it with itself.
concepts.c:cameron-martin-space: Only shifts in this space give an absolutely continuous translate.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: The norm $\|h'\|_{L^2}$ of the Hilbert space enters the density.
concepts.c:equivalent-measure: The conclusion is mutual absolute continuity of the two measures.
concepts.c:radon-nikodym-derivative: The theorem names the density of the shifted measure explicitly.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: Characteristic functions identify the finite-dimensional laws under $\nu$.
concepts.c:gaussian-measure: Both measures are Gaussian, so mean and covariance determine them.

source.note: The finite-dimensional proof of the Cameron-Martin formula, as in V. I. Bogachev, Gaussian Measures (AMS, 1998), chapter 2.

statement: Let $E$ be a [complete](c:complete-metric-space) normed abelian group, such as $\mathbb{R}$ or a [Banach space](c:banach-space). A family $(a_i)_{i \in I}$ in $E$ is summable if and only if its finite partial sums $s_F = \sum_{i \in F} a_i$ form a Cauchy [net](c:net): for every $\varepsilon > 0$ some finite $F_0$ has $\|s_F - s_G\| < \varepsilon$ for all finite $F, G \supseteq F_0$.

hypotheses.text: The group $E$ is [complete](c:complete-metric-space) for the metric $\|x - y\|$.

conclusion: The family $(a_i)$ is summable exactly when the net $(s_F)$ of its finite partial sums is Cauchy.

formal.difference: The declaration holds in any complete uniform space with a commutative additive monoid structure, so it is more general than the normed case stated here.

proofs.name: Cauchy nets in a complete space
proofs.slogan: A convergent net is Cauchy by the triangle inequality, and completeness turns a Cauchy net of partial sums into a convergent one.
proofs.scope: Both directions; the forward direction does not need completeness. An empty index set gives the zero family, which is summable with sum $0$.

roles.why: Completeness gives a limit for the Cauchy sequence of partial sums.

steps.slogan: Order the finite subsets $F \subseteq I$ by inclusion and form the net $s_F$.
steps.detail: The finite subsets form a directed set, since $F \cup G$ contains both $F$ and $G$. By definition, the family is summable with sum $s$ when the [net](c:net) $(s_F)$ converges to $s$.

steps.slogan: Show that a convergent net of partial sums is a Cauchy net.
steps.detail: If $s_F \to s$, choose a finite $F_0$ with $\|s_F - s\| < \varepsilon/2$ for all finite $F \supseteq F_0$. The triangle inequality gives $\|s_F - s_G\| < \varepsilon$ for all finite $F, G \supseteq F_0$.

steps.slogan: Extract an increasing chain $F_1 \subseteq F_2 \subseteq \dots$ of finite sets from the Cauchy net.
steps.detail: For each $k$ choose a finite $F_k$ with $\|s_F - s_G\| < 1/k$ for all finite $F, G \supseteq F_k$, and replace $F_k$ by $F_1 \cup \dots \cup F_k$. Then $(s_{F_k})$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence).

steps.slogan: Take the limit $s$ of the Cauchy sequence $(s_{F_k})$ by completeness.
steps.detail: Because $E$ is [complete](c:complete-metric-space), $s_{F_k} \to s$ for some $s \in E$. Letting $m \to \infty$ in $\|s_{F_m} - s_{F_k}\| < 1/k$ gives $\|s - s_{F_k}\| \le 1/k$.

steps.slogan: Show that the whole net of partial sums converges to $s$.
steps.detail: For finite $F \supseteq F_k$, $\|s_F - s\| \le \|s_F - s_{F_k}\| + \|s_{F_k} - s\| < 2/k$. So $s_F \to s$ and the family is summable; with step 2 this proves the equivalence.

concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness is exactly what makes Cauchy partial sums converge.
concepts.c:banach-space: Banach spaces are the main examples of complete normed groups.
concepts.c:net: Unordered partial sums are indexed by finite sets, so they form a net.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: A chain of finite sets turns the Cauchy net into a Cauchy sequence.

statement: Let $R > 0$ and let $f$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed disc $|z - c| \le R$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open disc $|z - c| < R$. Then the [contour integral](c:contour-integral) once counterclockwise around the circle satisfies $\oint_{|z - c| = R} \frac{f(z)}{(z - c)^2}\,dz = 2\pi i\, f'(c)$.

hypotheses.text: The radius satisfies $R > 0$.
The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed disc $|z - c| \le R$.
The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open disc $|z - c| < R$.

conclusion: The circle integral of $f(z)/(z - c)^2$ equals $2\pi i\, f'(c)$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values in any complex Banach space; for complex values it states the same.

proofs.name: Cauchy power series
proofs.slogan: Expand $f$ in a power series whose coefficients are circle integrals, and read off $f'(c)$ as the first coefficient.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Continuity up to the circle is what the Cauchy integral formula on the closed disc needs.

roles.why: A positive radius gives a genuine circle around $c$ and a disc with $c$ inside.
Continuity on the closed disc bounds $f$ on the circle and makes the Cauchy formula valid.
Holomorphy inside the disc gives the Cauchy integral formula.

steps.slogan: Write $f(w)$ by the Cauchy integral formula for every $w$ with $|w - c| < R$.
steps.detail: Continuity on the closed disc and holomorphy inside give $f(w) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z - c| = R} \frac{f(z)}{z - w}\,dz$ for every $w$ with $|w - c| < R$.

steps.slogan: Expand $1/(z - w)$ in a geometric series in $(w - c)/(z - c)$.
steps.detail: For $|z - c| = R$, $\frac{1}{z - w} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{(w - c)^n}{(z - c)^{n + 1}}$. The series converges uniformly in $z$ on the circle because $|w - c|/R < 1$.

steps.slogan: Integrate term by term to get a [power series](c:power-series) with circle-integral coefficients.
steps.detail: Uniform convergence and the boundedness of $f$ on the circle allow the exchange of sum and integral. So $f(w) = \sum_n a_n (w - c)^n$ with $a_n = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint \frac{f(z)}{(z - c)^{n + 1}}\,dz$.

steps.slogan: Read off the [complex derivative](c:complex-derivative) $f'(c)$ as the first coefficient $a_1$.
steps.detail: For small $h$, $f(c + h) - f(c) = a_1 h + h^2\sum_{n \ge 2} a_n h^{n - 2}$, and the last sum stays bounded. So $f'(c) = a_1$, and the formula for $a_1$ gives $\oint \frac{f(z)}{(z - c)^2}\,dz = 2\pi i\, f'(c)$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity up to the circle makes the boundary integral meaningful.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy inside the disc gives the Cauchy integral formula.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The derivative is expressed as an integral around the circle.
concepts.c:power-series: The Cauchy power series carries the derivative as its first coefficient.
concepts.c:complex-derivative: The formula computes the complex derivative at the centre.

proofs.name: Difference quotient under the integral
proofs.slogan: Write the difference quotient of $f$ at $c$ by the Cauchy formula and let the increment tend to zero under the integral sign.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with increments $|h| \le R/2$.

roles.why: A positive radius leaves room for increments $|h| \le R/2$ inside the disc.
Continuity on the closed disc bounds $f$ on the circle and makes the Cauchy formula valid.
Holomorphy inside the disc gives the Cauchy integral formula.

steps.slogan: Write $f(c)$ and $f(c + h)$ by the Cauchy integral formula on the circle.
steps.detail: For $|h| < R$, the Cauchy integral formula gives $f(c + h) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint \frac{f(z)}{z - c - h}\,dz$ and $f(c) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint \frac{f(z)}{z - c}\,dz$, both over $|z - c| = R$.

steps.slogan: Form the difference quotient of the two Cauchy integrals.
steps.detail: The identity $\frac{1}{z - c - h} - \frac{1}{z - c} = \frac{h}{(z - c - h)(z - c)}$ gives $\frac{f(c + h) - f(c)}{h} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint \frac{f(z)}{(z - c - h)(z - c)}\,dz$ for $0 < |h| \le R/2$.

steps.slogan: Let $h$ tend to zero under the integral by a uniform bound on the circle.
steps.detail: On $|z - c| = R$, the difference $\frac{1}{(z - c - h)(z - c)} - \frac{1}{(z - c)^2} = \frac{h}{(z - c - h)(z - c)^2}$ has modulus at most $2|h|/R^3$, and $f$ is bounded there. So the [contour integrals](c:contour-integral) converge, and the [complex derivative](c:complex-derivative) is $f'(c) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint \frac{f(z)}{(z - c)^2}\,dz$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity bounds $f$ on the circle for the uniform estimate.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy inside the disc gives the Cauchy integral formula.
concepts.c:contour-integral: Both values of $f$ and the limit are circle integrals.
concepts.c:complex-derivative: The limit of the difference quotient is the complex derivative.

source.note: The classical difference-quotient proof, as in L. V. Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, chapter 4.

statement: Let $R > 0$, let $f$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed disc $|z - c| \le R$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open disc, and let $|f(z)| \le M$ on the [circle](c:circle) $|z - c| = R$. Then $|f'(c)| \le M/R$.

hypotheses.text: The radius satisfies $R > 0$.
The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed disc $|z - c| \le R$.
The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open disc $|z - c| < R$.
The values on the circle satisfy $|f(z)| \le M$ for $|z - c| = R$.

conclusion: The [complex derivative](c:complex-derivative) at the centre satisfies $|f'(c)| \le M/R$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values in any complex normed space, complete or not; for complex values it states the same.

proofs.name: Estimate of the Cauchy integral
proofs.slogan: Write $f'(c)$ as a circle integral and bound the integrand by $M/R^2$ along a circle of length $2\pi R$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for complex values. For a general normed target, mathlib first maps the values into the completion so that the integral formula applies.

roles.why: A positive radius gives the circle and makes $M/R$ meaningful.
Continuity on the closed disc is needed for the Cauchy formula.
Holomorphy inside the disc gives the Cauchy formula for the derivative.
The bound on the circle bounds the integrand.

steps.slogan: Express $f'(c)$ by the Cauchy integral formula for the first derivative.
steps.detail: Continuity on the closed disc and holomorphy inside give $f'(c) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z - c| = R} \frac{f(z)}{(z - c)^2}\,dz$.

steps.slogan: Bound the integrand by $M/R^2$ on the circle.
steps.detail: For $|z - c| = R$, the integrand satisfies $\big|\frac{f(z)}{(z - c)^2}\big| = \frac{|f(z)|}{R^2} \le \frac{M}{R^2}$ by the bound on the [circle](c:circle).

steps.slogan: Multiply the bound by the circle length $2\pi R$ to bound the integral.
steps.detail: The modulus of a [contour integral](c:contour-integral) is at most the length of the path times the maximum of the integrand. So $|f'(c)| \le \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot 2\pi R\cdot\frac{M}{R^2} = \frac{M}{R}$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity up to the circle makes the Cauchy formula valid there.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives the integral formula for the derivative.
concepts.c:circle: The bound is assumed only on the boundary circle.
concepts.c:complex-derivative: The theorem bounds the complex derivative at the centre.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The length-times-maximum bound for the circle integral gives the estimate.

statement: Let $M, M', M''$ be [manifolds](c:manifold) with corners modelled on normed spaces over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $f\colon M \to M'$ and $g\colon M' \to M''$. If $f$ has [manifold derivative](c:manifold-derivative) $f'$ at $x$ and $g$ has manifold derivative $g'$ at $f(x)$, then $g \circ f$ has manifold derivative $g' \circ f'$ at $x$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f$ is continuous at $x$, and its expression in [charts](c:charted-space) at $x$ and $f(x)$ has [Fréchet derivative](c:frechet-derivative) $f'$ at the image of $x$.
The map $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$, and its expression in charts at $f(x)$ and $g(f(x))$ has Fréchet derivative $g'$ at the image of $f(x)$.

conclusion: The composite $g \circ f$ has manifold derivative $g' \circ f'$ from the [tangent space](c:tangent-space) $T_xM$ to $T_{g(f(x))}M''$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows any nontrivially normed field as the field of scalars.

proofs.name: Chain rule in charts
proofs.slogan: Write $g \circ f$ in charts as the composite of the chart expressions of $g$ and $f$ near $x$, and apply the chain rule for Fréchet derivatives.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Derivatives are taken within the range of the model with corners, which is the whole model space for manifolds without boundary.

roles.why: It gives continuity of $f$ at $x$ and the derivative $f'$ of the chart expression of $f$.
It gives continuity of $g$ at $f(x)$ and the derivative $g'$ of the chart expression of $g$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two continuity conditions to get continuity of $g \circ f$ at $x$.
steps.detail: The map $f$ is continuous at $x$ and $g$ is continuous at $f(x)$, so $g \circ f$ is continuous at $x$. This is the first half of the definition of a [manifold derivative](c:manifold-derivative).

steps.slogan: Find a neighbourhood of $x$ that $f$ maps into the chart domain at $f(x)$.
steps.detail: The [chart](c:charted-space) domain at $f(x)$ is an [open set](c:open-set) that contains $f(x)$, and $f$ is continuous at $x$. So its preimage under $f$ is a neighbourhood of $x$, and its image in the chart at $x$ is a neighbourhood of $\varphi(x)$ within the model range.

steps.slogan: Show that the chart expression of $g \circ f$ equals the composite of the chart expressions there.
steps.detail: Write $\tilde f = \psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ and $\tilde g = \chi \circ g \circ \psi^{-1}$. On the neighbourhood of step 2, $\psi^{-1}(\psi(f(y))) = f(y)$, so $\chi \circ (g \circ f) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \tilde g \circ \tilde f$ there.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $\tilde g \circ \tilde f$ by the chain rule for Fréchet derivatives.
steps.detail: The [Fréchet derivative](c:frechet-derivative) of $\tilde g$ at $\tilde f(\varphi(x)) = \psi(f(x))$ is $g'$, and that of $\tilde f$ at $\varphi(x)$ is $f'$. The chain rule gives the derivative $g' \circ f'$ for $\tilde g \circ \tilde f$, and step 3 passes it to the chart expression of $g \circ f$, because a derivative depends only on a neighbourhood.

steps.slogan: Join continuity and the chart derivative into the manifold derivative of $g \circ f$.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 4 are the two conditions in the definition of a manifold derivative. So $g \circ f$ has manifold derivative $g' \circ f'$ from the [tangent space](c:tangent-space) at $x$ to the one at $g(f(x))$.

concepts.c:manifold: The maps act between manifolds, so derivatives are read in charts.
concepts.c:manifold-derivative: The theorem computes the manifold derivative of a composite map.
concepts.c:tangent-space: The derivatives are linear maps between tangent spaces.
concepts.c:charted-space: Charts turn the maps into maps between normed spaces.
concepts.c:frechet-derivative: In charts the manifold derivative is a Fréchet derivative.
concepts.c:open-set: The open chart domain gives the neighbourhood where charts cancel.

statement: A subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is [connected](c:connected-space) (the empty set included) if and only if it is an [interval](c:interval): $\emptyset$, $\mathbb{R}$, $[a, b]$ with $a \le b$, $[a, b)$, $(a, b]$ or $(a, b)$ with $a < b$, or $[a, \infty)$, $(a, \infty)$, $(-\infty, b]$, $(-\infty, b)$. Distinct entries of this list are distinct sets.

hypotheses.text: The set $S$ lies in the [real numbers](c:real-number) with their usual order topology.

conclusion: The connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the sets of the list, each given by one type and one choice of endpoints.

formal.difference: The declaration classifies preconnected sets in any densely ordered, conditionally complete linear order with the order topology, and its list has repeats such as $\emptyset = (a, a)$. It does not state that distinct entries give distinct sets.

proofs.name: Order-convexity and suprema
proofs.slogan: Show that connected sets contain every point between two of their points, classify such sets by infimum and supremum, and prove each interval connected by a supremum argument.
proofs.scope: The whole classification, with $\emptyset$ counted as connected as in mathlib. A reader who requires connected sets to be nonempty drops $\emptyset$ from the list.

roles.why: Completeness and density of $\mathbb{R}$ supply the infimum, the supremum and the point $s$ of the argument.

steps.slogan: Show that a connected set contains every point between two of its points.
steps.detail: Let $x < c < y$ with $x, y \in S$ and $c \notin S$. Then $S \cap (-\infty, c)$ and $S \cap (c, \infty)$ are disjoint, relatively open, nonempty and cover $S$, so $S$ is not [connected](c:connected-space).

steps.slogan: Classify an order-convex set by its infimum, its supremum and whether it contains them.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be nonempty with $a = \inf S \in [-\infty, \infty)$ and $b = \sup S \in (-\infty, \infty]$, which exist by the [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) property. Order-convexity gives $(a, b) \subseteq S \subseteq [a, b]$, so $S$ is the [interval](c:interval) with ends $a, b$ that contains exactly those finite ends that lie in $S$.

steps.slogan: Show that the infimum, the supremum and the end types determine the entry.
steps.detail: Each entry of the list has its left end as infimum and its right end as supremum, and it contains a finite end exactly when its bracket is closed. The condition $a < b$ for the non-closed bounded types excludes empty duplicates, so different entries are different sets.

steps.slogan: Prove that each interval is connected by a supremum argument.
steps.detail: Suppose an interval $I = U \cup V$ with $U, V$ disjoint, nonempty and relatively open, and $x \in U$, $y \in V$, $x < y$. Let $s = \sup\{t \in [x, y] : [x, t] \subseteq U\}$; then $s \in I$, and openness of $U$ or of $V$ near $s$ contradicts the choice of $s$.

steps.slogan: Join both directions and the uniqueness into the classification.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 put every connected set in the list, step 4 shows that every entry is connected, and step 3 shows that the list has no repeats.

concepts.c:connected-space: The theorem lists exactly the connected subsets of the line.
concepts.c:interval: Intervals are the answer of the classification.
concepts.c:real-number: Completeness and density of the reals drive both directions.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: Infimum and supremum fix the ends of each interval.

statement: Let $X$ be a [first-countable space](c:first-countable-space), $\mu$ a measure on $[a, b]$ and $F\colon X \times [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$. If each $F(x, \cdot)$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function), $|F(x, t)| \le g(t)$ for all $x$ and almost every $t$ with $g$ [integrable](c:integrable-function), and $x \mapsto F(x, t)$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) for almost every $t$, then $x \mapsto \int_a^b F(x, t)\,d\mu(t)$ is continuous.

hypotheses.text: The parameter space $X$ is [first-countable](c:first-countable-space), for example a metric space.
For each $x$, the function $t \mapsto F(x, t)$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function) on $[a, b]$.
Some $\mu$-[integrable](c:integrable-function) $g$ on $[a, b]$ satisfies $|F(x, t)| \le g(t)$ for every $x$ and almost every $t$.
For almost every $t$, the function $x \mapsto F(x, t)$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

conclusion: The function $x \mapsto \int_a^b F(x, t)\,d\mu(t)$ is continuous on $X$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values in any real normed space and integrates over the oriented interval from $a$ to $b$. Its hypotheses are stated almost everywhere on $(\min(a, b), \max(a, b)]$.

proofs.name: Dominated convergence along sequences
proofs.slogan: Check continuity along convergent sequences of parameters and pass to the limit under the integral by dominated convergence.
proofs.scope: Continuity at every point $x_0 \in X$. The bound may fail on a null set that depends on $x$; only countably many $x_n$ enter, so this is harmless.

roles.why: First countability reduces continuity to convergence along sequences.
Measurability makes each $F(x_n, \cdot)$ a candidate for dominated convergence.
The integrable bound dominates every $F(x_n, \cdot)$.
Continuity in $x$ for almost every $t$ gives the pointwise limit.

steps.slogan: Reduce continuity at $x_0$ to convergence along sequences $x_n \to x_0$.
steps.detail: In a [first-countable space](c:first-countable-space), a function is continuous at $x_0$ when it maps every sequence $x_n \to x_0$ to a sequence that converges to its value at $x_0$. So fix such a sequence.

steps.slogan: Show that $F(x_n, t) \to F(x_0, t)$ for almost every $t$.
steps.detail: Outside one null set of $t$, the function $x \mapsto F(x, t)$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function). For these $t$, $x_n \to x_0$ gives $F(x_n, t) \to F(x_0, t)$.

steps.slogan: Bound all the functions $F(x_n, \cdot)$ by the one integrable function $g$.
steps.detail: For each $n$, $|F(x_n, t)| \le g(t)$ outside a null set $N_n$. The countable union of the sets $N_n$ is null, so the bound holds for all $n$ at almost every $t$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit under the [integral](c:integral) by dominated convergence.
steps.detail: The functions $F(x_n, \cdot)$ are [measurable](c:measurable-function), converge almost everywhere by step 2, and are dominated by the [integrable](c:integrable-function) $g$ by step 3. The dominated convergence theorem gives $\int_a^b F(x_n, t)\,d\mu \to \int_a^b F(x_0, t)\,d\mu$, so the integral is continuous at $x_0$.

concepts.c:first-countable-space: First countability lets sequences test continuity.
concepts.c:integrable-function: The integrable bound is the dominating function.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity in the parameter gives pointwise convergence of integrands.
concepts.c:integral: The theorem concerns an integral that depends on a parameter.

source.note: mathlib applies continuousAt_of_dominated_interval at each point, which uses dominated convergence along the neighbourhood filter, countably generated by first countability.

statement: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space) and $f_n\colon X \to E$ [continuous](c:continuous-function) functions into a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $E$. If $\|f_n(x)\| \le u_n$ for all $n$ and $x$, with $\sum_n u_n < \infty$ (a [summable bound](c:summable-bound)), then $x \mapsto \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n(x)$ is continuous.

hypotheses.text: Each function $f_n$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).
The target $E$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), or any complete normed abelian group.
The numbers $u_n$ satisfy $\|f_n(x)\| \le u_n$ for all $x$ and $\sum_n u_n < \infty$.

conclusion: The sum $S(x) = \sum_n f_n(x)$ exists for every $x$ and is continuous on $X$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows any index type, with unconditional sums, and a complete normed abelian group as target; for the index set $\mathbb{N}$ it states the same.

proofs.name: Weierstrass M-test and uniform limit
proofs.slogan: The summable bound makes the partial sums converge uniformly, and a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for empty $X$ there is nothing to prove.

roles.why: Continuity of each term makes every partial sum continuous.
Completeness makes the absolutely convergent series converge.
The summable bound controls the series at each point and the tails uniformly.

steps.slogan: Show that the series converges at each point by absolute convergence.
steps.detail: At each $x$, $\sum_n \|f_n(x)\| \le \sum_n u_n < \infty$. An [absolutely convergent](c:absolute-convergence) series in a complete space converges, so $S(x)$ exists.

steps.slogan: Bound the tails of the series uniformly by the tails of $\sum u_n$.
steps.detail: For every $x$, $\|S(x) - \sum_{n < N} f_n(x)\| \le \sum_{n \ge N} u_n$, which tends to $0$ independently of $x$. So the partial sums converge [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) to $S$.

steps.slogan: Show that each partial sum is continuous as a finite sum.
steps.detail: Addition in a normed space is continuous, so a finite sum of continuous functions is continuous. Hence every partial sum $S_N = \sum_{n < N} f_n$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Pass continuity to the uniform limit by a three-epsilon estimate.
steps.detail: Given $x_0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $N$ with $\|S - S_N\| < \varepsilon/3$ on $X$ and a neighbourhood $U$ of $x_0$ with $\|S_N(x) - S_N(x_0)\| < \varepsilon/3$ on $U$. Then $\|S(x) - S(x_0)\| < \varepsilon$ on $U$.

concepts.c:topological-space: Continuity on a general topological space needs only neighbourhoods.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity passes from the terms to the sum.
concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of the target makes the series converge.
concepts.c:summable-bound: The summable bound is the M-test hypothesis.
concepts.c:absolute-convergence: Absolute convergence gives the sum at each point.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence carries continuity to the limit.
